fetched_contents.text: Explicating peer feedback quality and its impact on feedback implementation in EFL writing Abstract Introduction Although it is commonly acknowledged that peer feedback quality is crucial to the success of peer review, there is a lack of consensus on how it could be determined. More importantly, how feedback quality interacts with other factors like feedback features and focus, and ultimately influences peer feedback implementation remains insufficiently investigated. Methods The present study examined peer feedback quality and its impact on Chinese students’ feedback implementation in two argumentative writing tasks. Peer feedback quality was measured according to a self-designed two-dimensional measurement scale: accuracy and revision potential. Results Quantitative analyses of 5,606 implementable idea units of feedback and 440 writing drafts by 110 students revealed that feedback accuracy was at a medium level and revision potential was at a low level, with accuracy demonstrating stronger predictive power on implementation; the predictive strengths of feedback accuracy and revision potential were strongest when feedback features and focus were considered; the overall peer feedback quality was low and medium-quality feedback was implemented most frequently; feedback quality significantly and most strongly predicted implementation in combination with feedback features and focus. Discussion The study highlights the importance of future instructions in training students to provide and implement high-quality feedback with good accuracy and high revision potential. Keywords: peer feedback quality, accuracy, revision potential, implementation, EFL writing Introduction Despite the proliferation of studies on peer feedback over the past three decades (Tsui and Ng, 2000; Wu, 2019; Cui et al., 2021; Payant and Zuniga, 2022), doubts about the effectiveness of peer feedback remain constant “as students are not experts in a subject area, peer feedback is susceptible to variation” (Strijbos et al., 2010, p. 291). In particular, although the large class size in EFL contexts like China has necessitated the use of peer feedback as a complement to teacher feedback in writing courses (Hu and Zhang, 2014; Wu et al., 2022), this skepticism on feedback quality (Nilson, 2003; Gielen et al., 2010) has hindered the application of this instructional activity in such contexts. The importance of peer feedback quality has been widely acknowledged (Hattie and Timperley, 2007; Walker, 2015; Rotsaert et al., 2018), but it has not been defined consistently in the literature (Rosalia and Llosa, 2009; Gielen et al., 2010; Hovardas et al., 2014). Generally, conceptualizations of feedback quality have shifted from a comment-centric perspective concentrating on the features, amount, and length of feedback (e.g., Sluijsmans et al., 2002; Prins et al., 2006; Patchan et al., 2018; Rotsaert et al., 2018) to a text-centric perspective which takes alignment and accuracy of peer feedback to text problems as central to feedback quality (e.g., van Steendam et al., 2010; Hovardas et al., 2014; Gao et al., 2019). More recently, feedback quality has been defined functionally by integrating problem detection accuracy with the usefulness of suggested solutions based on whether a comment could improve essay quality measurably on rubrics (Wu and Schunn, 2020a). As success in peer review mostly relies on the use of feedback in subsequent revision/feedback implementation (van der Pol et al., 2008; Dressler et al., 2019), this integrative definition well highlights the significance of peer feedback in promoting the writing improvement. However, to capture more dimensions of peer feedback quality, a more detailed measurement is needed. Previous measurement scales from a comment-centric perspective generally focused on feedback types, features, and whether the feedback met certain assessment criteria (Prins et al., 2006; Walker, 2015), but they did not empirically test the contribution of the identified feedback characteristics on performance (Gielen et al., 2010). Thus, it is necessary to develop a comprehensive measurement scale that speaks specifically to the potential effect of peer feedback. Additionally, although feedback quality has been reported to determine implementation (van der Pol et al., 2008; Wu and Schunn, 2020a), it is still difficult to assume that this relationship would be similar in L2 writing classrooms, considering that language and culture may provide expected challenges (Carson and Nelson, 1994; Ramanathan and Atkinson, 1999; Lundstrom and Baker, 2009). Therefore, in this study with Chinese EFL learners writing English argumentative essays, we intended to explicate peer feedback quality in measurable ways and test its impact on feedback implementation since using feedback to revise is central to peer review. Unlike most measurements concentrating on the characteristics of peer feedback (e.g., Sluijsmans et al., 2002; Prins et al., 2006), the current study focused on feedback content which can critically influence its effectiveness (Anson and Anson, 2017). We also considered two factors crucial to implementation: feedback features and focus, given that the revision process based on peer feedback is complex and feedback implementation is influenced by many factors (Wu and Schunn, 2020a). Specifically, we investigated whether considering these two factors would change the existing effect of feedback quality on feedback implementation. fetched_contents.text: Teaching Students to Evaluate Each Other Why use peer review? Peer assessment, or review, can improve overall learning by helping students become better readers, writers, and collaborators. A well-designed peer review program also develops students’ evaluation and assessment skills. The following are a few techniques that instructors have used to implement peer review. Planning for peer review * Identify where you can incorporate peer review exercises into your course. * For peer review on written assignments, design guidelines that specify clearly defined tasks for the reviewer. Consider what feedback students can competently provide. * Determine whether peer review activities will be conducted as in-class or out-of-class assignments (or as a combination of both). * Plan for in-class peer reviews to last at least one class session. More time will be needed for longer papers and papers written in foreign languages. * Model appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback through the comments you provide on papers and in class. * Explain the reasons for peer review, the benefits it provides, and how it supports course learning outcomes. * Set clear expectations: determine whether students will receive grades on their contributions to peer review sessions. If grades are given, be clear about what you are assessing, what criteria will be used for grading, and how the peer review score will be incorporated into their overall course grade. Before the first peer review session * Give students a sample paper to review and comment on in class using the peer review guidelines. Ask students to share feedback and help them rephrase their comments to make them more specific and constructive, as needed. * Consider using the sample paper exercise to teach students how to think about, respond to, and use comments by peer reviewers to improve their writing. * Ask for input from students on the peer review worksheet or co-create a rubric in class. * Prevent overly harsh peer criticism by instructing students to provide feedback as if they were speaking to the writer or presenter directly. * Consider how you will assign students to groups. Do you want them to work together for the entire semester, or change for different assignments? Do you want peer reviewers to remain anonymous? How many reviews will each assignment receive? During and after peer review sessions * Give clear directions and time limits for in-class peer review sessions and set defined deadlines for out-of-class peer review assignments. * Listen to group discussions and provide guidance and input when necessary. * Consider requiring students to write a plan for revision indicating the changes they intend to make on the paper and explaining why they have chosen to acknowledge or disregard specific comments and suggestions. For exams and presentations, have students write about how they would approach the task next time based on the peer comments. * Ask students to submit the peer feedback they received with their final papers. Make clear whether or not you will be taking this feedback into account when grading the paper, or when assigning a participation grade to the student reviewer. * Consider having students assess the quality of the feedback they received. * Discuss the process in class, addressing problems that were encountered and what was learned. Examples of peer review activities * After collection, redistribute papers randomly along with a grading rubric. After students have evaluated the papers ask them to exchange with a neighbor, evaluate the new paper, and then compare notes. * After completing an exam, have students compare and discuss answers with a partner. You may offer them the opportunity to submit a new answer, dividing points between the two. * In a small class, ask students to bring one copy of their paper with their name on it and one or two copies without a name. Collect the “name” copy and redistribute the others for peer review. Provide feedback on all student papers. Collect the peer reviews and return papers to their authors. * For group presentations, require the class to evaluate the group’s performance using a predetermined marking scheme. * When working on group projects, have students evaluate each group member’s contribution to the project on a scale of 1-10. Require students to provide rationale for how and why they awarded points. fetched_contents.text: The role and features of peer assessment feedback in college English writing Abstract Peer assessment is a common pedagogical practice for evaluating students’ writing in college English classrooms. However, in-depth research on the learning outcomes after peer assessment is scarce and inconsistent; how peer feedback is used has not been fully explored either. This study compared peer feedback to teacher feedback and explored the different features of feedback and its impact on draft revision. Two specific research questions were answered in this study: (1) In which aspects can peer feedback supplement teacher feedback in improving the linguistic features in writing? (2) What are the differences in features of peer feedback versus teacher feedback? And how do they connect to feedback take-in? Two writing tasks were assigned to 94 students. One received teacher feedback and the other peer feedback. Pre-feedback and post-feedback writings in both tasks (4 sets in total) were scored and human ratings were adjusted using Many-Facet Rasch modeling to control for differences in leniency. Drawing on three natural language processing (NLP) tools, this study also assessed writing qualities by comparing 22 selected indices related to the scoring rubrics for human raters, which involve three dimensions: cohesion, lexical quality and syntactic complexity. Peer and teacher feedback was then coded based on features of feedback to explore their influence on draft revision. The results showed that both peer and teacher feedback had positive effects on rating scores. We confirmed peer feedback as an effective classroom approach to improve writing, though limited compared to teacher feedback as reflected in the indices. In terms of feedback features, students often stopped at identifying the language problems, while the teacher provided more explanations, solutions or suggestions regarding the problems identified. Implications for peer feedback research and implementation of peer assessment activities are provided. Peer assessment has also been acknowledged as an approach to delivering feedback to students in an efficient and effective manner (Topping, 1998; van Zundert et al., 2010). A substantial amount of research has been conducted on the role and benefits of peer assessment from various aspects, including its influence on students’ writing self-efficacy (e.g., Fathi et al., 2019; Lee and Evans, 2019), autonomous motivation (e.g., Yousefifard and Fathi, 2021), and writing performance (e.g., Nelson and Schunn, 2009). Accordingly, this study decides to examine the effects of peer feedback from a different perspective by comparing its role against teacher feedback. It also looks into the feedback features of peer review in the feedback process and compares to those by the classroom teacher for a more valid evaluation of feedback impacts. We hope to illuminate both researchers and teachers on an efficacious deployment of peer assessment in English as a foreign language (EFL) classroom settings, focusing on writing progress. It is necessary to distinguish it from peer assessment for the current study. According to Liu and Carless (2006), peer feedback refers to a “communication process through which learners enter into dialogues related to performance and standards” (p. 2). Despite this process-centric interpretation, it is also conceptualized as the “information learners can use to improve the quality of their work or learning strategies” (Winstone et al., 2022, p. 224). Peer assessment is defined as “an arrangement for learners to consider and specify the level, value, or quality of a product or performance of other equal-status learners, then learn further by giving elaborated feedback and discussing their judgments with peers to achieve a negotiated agreed outcome” (Topping, 2017, p. 2). Therefore, the distinction between the two terms lies in that peer feedback is about the communication process and all the concrete information produced in this process, such as direct error correction or simply comments, but without a formal score; whereas peer assessment involves both peer feedback and a final grading. In this study, for example, peer assessment is the activity that generated rating scores in addition to feedback in words that justified the ratings. The latter is the focus of this study. Branch on assessment design and classroom support for peer feedback

This branch shows that effective peer feedback depends on thoughtful design, scaffolding, teacher modeling, and accountability. The evidence points to structured formats and gradual scaffolding as key usability improvements. For example, the peer assessment feedback study emphasizes that peer feedback is a “structured process where students assess each other’s work using clear success criteria” and that scaffolding can support learners, especially low-proficiency second-language students, by providing small steps and sentence starters [N4-R4][N4-R5]. The same study also notes that peer feedback is often used to supplement teacher feedback in high-stakes EFL settings, but its effectiveness is limited compared to teacher feedback, which suggests that classroom design must balance student participation with teacher support [N4-F3].

Feedback formats and scaffolding improve usability by making the process more concrete. The peer feedback scaffold described in the evidence includes “small steps for those introducing feedback in their classrooms” and “T-A-G sentence starters,” which help students navigate the process without being overwhelmed [N4-R5]. The college English writing study similarly frames peer assessment as a common pedagogical practice, but it also highlights that feedback features matter, including whether students identify language problems versus whether teachers provide explanations and solutions [N4-F3]. This implies that scaffolding should not just be procedural; it should also support students in distinguishing between problem recognition and solution-oriented feedback.

Teacher modeling and guided practice are central to classroom support. The Cornell teaching guide explicitly says instructors should “model appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback” and “explain the reasons for peer review, the benefits it provides, and how it supports course learning outcomes” [N3-F2]. It also recommends using sample papers and peer review worksheets to teach students how to think about, respond to, and use comments, which is a form of guided practice [N3-F2]. The study on rubric co-construction further supports this by showing that co-created rubrics can be used in conjunction with worksheets for self and peer assessment, suggesting that rubrics are a practical way to guide evaluation [N3-R2]. The evidence also stresses that in-class peer review sessions should last at least one class session and that longer papers or foreign-language papers need more time, which reinforces the need for structured time and teacher oversight [N3-F2].

Grading and accountability shape student engagement by making participation meaningful. The Cornell guide notes that instructors should decide whether students will receive grades for their contributions and should be clear about what is assessed, what criteria are used, and how peer review scores are incorporated into the course grade [N3-F2]. It also says students should submit peer feedback with their final papers and that instructors should make clear whether this feedback will be taken into account, which ties accountability to both student responsibility and teacher transparency [N3-F2]. The peer feedback quality study further shows that feedback implementation is strongly affected by feedback quality and features, implying that grading can influence how seriously students treat peer review [N1-F1]. Taken together, these sources suggest that accountability mechanisms should be explicit, fair, and aligned with course goals to sustain student engagement.

Overall, the evidence supports a design-oriented view of peer feedback: use structured formats and scaffolding to make the process usable, model and guide students through practice, and use grading and accountability to create motivation and responsibility [N4-R4][N4-R5][N3-F2][N4-F3].

Branch on how to teach students to evaluate writing more effectively

This branch shows that teaching students to evaluate writing more effectively requires specific criteria, rubric-based instruction, practice routines, and strategies to distinguish helpful from unhelpful feedback. The strongest evidence comes from the practical teaching guide, which frames peer review as a way to improve learning by helping students become better readers, writers, and collaborators and stresses that a well-designed peer review program develops evaluation and assessment skills [N3-F2]. It also provides concrete strategies: planning peer review exercises, designing guidelines for reviewers, modeling constructive criticism, and making clear expectations about grading and participation [N3-F2].

Specific evaluative criteria and rubric-based instruction are central. The Cornell guide explicitly recommends using clearly defined tasks for reviewers and considering what feedback students can competently provide [N3-F2]. It also mentions co-created rubrics and worksheets for self and peer assessment, which align with rubric-based instruction [N3-R2]. The same study notes that rubrics are often used as scoring tools in evaluating writing performance, which supports the idea that rubrics can anchor evaluation rather than merely summarize quality [N3-R1]. The peer assessment feedback study similarly discusses feedback features and rubric-related indices, reinforcing that evaluation is best supported by explicit criteria and feedback dimensions [N4-F3]. Together, these sources indicate that instruction should start with clear criteria and rubric-based frameworks so students know what to look for.

Practice routines that build confidence and accuracy are important because students need repeated exposure to the evaluation process. The Cornell guide recommends using sample papers, having students share feedback, and asking them to rephrase comments to make them more specific and constructive [N3-F2]. It also suggests requiring students to write a revision plan and explain why they choose to acknowledge or disregard specific comments, which turns feedback into a learning task rather than a one-time exercise [N3-F2]. The peer feedback quality study further shows that feedback accuracy is a key dimension and that revision potential is also important, implying that practice should target both detecting problems and suggesting improvements [N1-F1]. This aligns with the idea that practice routines should be iterative, scaffolded, and tied to revision.

Ways to help students distinguish helpful from unhelpful feedback are also covered in the evidence. The Cornell guide advises instructors to “prevent overly harsh peer criticism” by instructing students to provide feedback as if they were speaking directly to the writer [N3-F2]. It also emphasizes modeling appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback, which helps students avoid vague or judgmental comments [N3-F2]. The peer assessment feedback study adds that students often stop at identifying language problems while teachers provide more explanations, solutions, or suggestions [N4-F3]. This suggests a teaching strategy: helping students move beyond simple problem detection to solution-oriented feedback. The evidence also supports training in peer review skills as a way to improve this ability, though a separate review notes that formal training is scarce in higher education [N5-R3]. Taken together, the evidence implies that students need explicit instruction on what makes feedback helpful versus unhelpful, plus practice in applying those standards.

Overall, the evidence supports a three-part approach: teach specific criteria and rubric-based evaluation, provide guided practice routines to build confidence and accuracy, and explicitly train students to identify helpful versus unhelpful feedback [N3-F2][N3-R2][N4-F3][N5-R3].

This branch identifies three main barriers: language limitations and metalinguistic knowledge, task complexity and writing type, and student and teacher attitudes. The evidence shows that these factors interact to reduce feedback quality and weaken peer feedback use.

Language limitations and metalinguistic knowledge reduce feedback quality because students may not have the vocabulary or conceptual tools to provide accurate or useful comments. The peer feedback quality study notes that feedback quality is central to peer review, but it also emphasizes that language and culture may provide expected challenges in L2 writing classrooms [N1-F1]. It further reports that feedback accuracy was medium and revision potential was low, with accuracy showing stronger predictive power on implementation [N1-F1]. The study also says that feedback features and focus were important predictors, indicating that students’ language proficiency affects not only what they can say but also how effectively they can frame their comments [N1-F1]. The scaffolding study adds that low-proficiency second-language students can improve writing by giving and receiving peer feedback, which implies that language barriers can both hinder and be addressed through scaffolding [N2-R1]. Together, these sources suggest that students with weaker language and metalinguistic skills are more likely to produce less accurate and less helpful feedback.

Task complexity and writing type matter because they change how difficult it is for students to evaluate writing. The peer assessment feedback study compares peer feedback to teacher feedback and explores how different feedback features and task contexts affect draft revision [N4-F3]. It also notes that peer feedback was found to have positive effects, though limited compared to teacher feedback, which implies that the difficulty of the writing task influences feedback effectiveness [N4-F3]. The study further says that students often stopped at identifying language problems while teachers provided more explanations, solutions, or suggestions, which suggests that more complex writing or more demanding tasks may require more sophisticated feedback [N4-F3]. The peer feedback quality study also reports that feedback implementation depends on feedback features and focus, so task complexity likely affects what students can detect and what they can usefully comment on [N1-F1]. Taken together, the evidence indicates that feedback difficulty rises with task complexity and writing type, and that students may struggle to move beyond basic problem identification.

Common student and teacher attitudes weaken peer feedback use. Student attitudes are highlighted by the study on peer feedback quality, which notes that feedback quality remains an important but inconsistently defined concept and that low-quality feedback is implemented most frequently [N1-F1]. The study also emphasizes that feedback implementation is influenced by many factors, including feedback features and focus, which implies that students’ willingness or ability to act on feedback can be shaped by their perceptions [N1-F1]. The student perceptions study explicitly explores student perceptions and experiences of peer review, the influences on potential feedback uptake, and the value attributed to discourse, showing that attitudes and experiences matter for uptake [N6-R1]. Another study on student beliefs and orientations toward peer feedback states that the effectiveness of peer feedback likely depends on students’ beliefs and orientations [N6-R2]. The student attitude study likewise reports that students with different attitudes perform and uptake peer feedback differently [N6-R3]. These findings together show that negative or uncertain beliefs can reduce uptake, while positive attitudes can support participation.

Teacher attitudes and classroom practices also matter. The scaffolding study notes that peer feedback is often used in large EFL classes as a complement to teacher feedback because of class size and the need for frequent, detailed feedback [N4-F3]. However, the same study says skepticism about feedback quality has hindered application in such contexts [N4-F3]. The peer feedback quality study similarly states that doubts about peer feedback remain constant because students are not subject-area experts, and skepticism about quality has limited use [N1-F1]. This suggests that teachers’ own attitudes and classroom design choices can either support or weaken peer feedback. The Cornell teaching guide also notes that instructors should explain the reasons for peer review and how it supports learning outcomes, indicating that teacher support can counteract reluctance and improve uptake [N3-F2].

Overall, the evidence shows that peer feedback is limited by students’ language and metalinguistic ability, by the complexity and type of writing tasks, and by students’ and teachers’ attitudes toward feedback. These barriers combine to make peer feedback less effective unless carefully managed [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3].

### 1) Language limitations and metalinguistic knowledge reduce feedback quality
A major barrier is that students’ language proficiency and metalinguistic knowledge affect how well they can provide useful feedback. The peer feedback quality study explicitly notes that language and culture may provide expected challenges in L2 writing classrooms, and it reports that feedback accuracy was medium while revision potential was low, with accuracy showing stronger predictive power on implementation [N1-F1]. The branch reports show that students’ evaluative skills can be improved through **specific criteria and rubric-based instruction**, **practice routines that build confidence and accuracy**, and **explicit training to distinguish helpful from unhelpful feedback**.

It also mentions co-created rubrics and worksheets for self and peer assessment, which support rubric-based instruction [N3-R2]. The peer assessment feedback study similarly discusses feedback features and rubric-related indices, reinforcing that evaluation is best supported by explicit criteria [N4-F3]. ### 2) Build confidence and accuracy through practice routines

The Cornell guide recommends using sample papers, having students share feedback, and asking them to rephrase comments to make them more specific and constructive [N3-F2]. The Cornell guide advises instructors to “prevent overly harsh peer criticism” by instructing students to provide feedback as if they were speaking directly to the writer [N3-F2]. It also emphasizes modeling appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback, which helps students avoid vague or judgmental comments [N3-F2]. The branch on student uptake and motivation shows that engagement depends on **perceptions, experiences, and training**, with training and feedback literacy playing a key role.

The evidence suggests that peer feedback is encouraged when it is structured, supported, and relevant. ## How assessment design and classroom support can make peer feedback more usable

The branch on assessment design and classroom support shows that peer feedback is more effective when it is **structured, scaffolded, modeled, and accountable**.

Feedback should be structured so students can navigate the process. ### 2) Teacher modeling and guided practice are essential
Teachers should model appropriate feedback and guide students through the process. The Cornell guide explicitly says instructors should “model appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback” and “explain the reasons for peer review, the benefits it provides, and how it supports course learning outcomes” [N3-F2]. The evidence suggests that peer feedback is encouraged when it is structured, supported, and relevant. The student perceptions study notes that students prefer direct and individualized feedback and that trust is important [N6-R5]. The peer feedback quality study also shows that low-quality feedback is implemented most frequently, so quality matters for uptake [N1-F1]. Overall, the main challenges limiting peer feedback in ESL writing classrooms are **language limitations and metalinguistic knowledge**, **task complexity and writing type**, and **students’ and teachers’ attitudes**. ## How assessment design and classroom support can make peer feedback more usable

The branch on assessment design and classroom support shows that peer feedback is more effective when it is **structured, scaffolded, modeled, and accountable**.

### 1) Feedback formats and scaffolding improve usability
Feedback should be structured so students can navigate the process. The evidence emphasizes that peer feedback is a “structured process where students assess each other’s work using clear success criteria” [N4-R4]. Scaffolding is also central: the T-A-G Peer Feedback scaffold provides small steps for those introducing feedback in their classrooms, including sentence starters [N4-R5]. This makes the process more concrete and reduces the cognitive load on learners. The peer assessment feedback study likewise shows that peer feedback is often used to supplement teacher feedback in EFL settings, but that its effectiveness is limited compared to teacher feedback [N4-F3]. This supports a design approach that balances student participation with teacher support.

### 2) Teacher modeling and guided practice are essential
Teachers should model appropriate feedback and guide students through the process. The Cornell guide explicitly says instructors should “model appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback” and “explain the reasons for peer review, the benefits it provides, and how it supports course learning outcomes” [N3-F2]. It also recommends using sample papers and peer review worksheets to teach students how to think about, respond to, and use comments [N3-F2]. The scaffolding study similarly supports the use of small steps and sentence starters as a way to scaffold learners [N4-R5]. Modeling and guided practice help students internalize evaluation standards and reduce dependency on teacher correction.

### 3) Grading and accountability shape student engagement
Grading and accountability make peer feedback meaningful. The Cornell guide notes that instructors should decide whether students will receive grades for their contributions and be clear about what is assessed, what criteria are used, and how peer review scores are incorporated into the course grade [N3-F2]. It also says students should submit peer feedback with their final papers and that instructors should make clear whether this feedback will be taken into account, which ties accountability to both student responsibility and teacher transparency [N3-F2]. The peer feedback quality study further shows that feedback implementation is strongly affected by feedback quality and features [N1-F1], implying that grading can influence how seriously students treat peer review.

## How student uptake and motivation can be improved

The branch on student uptake and motivation shows that engagement depends on **perceptions, experiences, and training**, with training and feedback literacy playing a key role.

### 1) Student perceptions and experiences shape uptake
Students are more likely to give and receive peer feedback when they perceive it as useful and trustworthy. The student perceptions study directly explores student perceptions and experiences of peer review, the influences on potential feedback uptake, and the value attributed to discourse [N6-R1]. It also reports that students prefer direct and individualized feedback and that trust in the teacher-student relationship is crucial for effective feedback uptake [N6-R5]. The student attitude study further shows that students with different attitudes perform and uptake peer feedback differently [N6-R3]. This means that classroom experiences and beliefs are central to whether students participate.

### 2) What encourages or discourages feedback uptake
The evidence suggests that peer feedback is encouraged when it is structured, supported, and relevant. The student perceptions study notes that students prefer direct and individualized feedback and that trust is important [N6-R5]. The peer feedback quality study also shows that low-quality feedback is implemented most frequently, so quality matters for uptake [N1-F1]. The scaffolding study indicates that peer feedback is often used in large EFL classes because of class size and the need for frequent, detailed feedback, but that skepticism about quality can limit use [N4-F3]. Taken together, peer feedback is likely to be motivating when it is meaningful and trustworthy, and discouraging when students doubt its value or quality.

### 3) Training and feedback literacy matter for engagement
Students need training in feedback literacy to engage effectively. The Cornell guide recommends teaching students how to think about, respond to, and use comments by peer reviewers [N3-F2]. It also advises instructors to model appropriate constructive criticism and descriptive feedback, and to give clear directions and time limits for peer review sessions [N3-F2]. The study on rubric co-construction further supports this by showing that co-created rubrics and worksheets can be used in conjunction with self and peer assessment [N3-R2]. The peer feedback quality study adds that feedback quality and features are important predictors of implementation, so training should target both content and form [N1-F1]. When students are trained in feedback literacy, they are more likely to treat peer review as a learning process rather than a passive activity.

## Integrated conclusion

Overall, the main challenges limiting peer feedback in ESL writing classrooms are **language limitations and metalinguistic knowledge**, **task complexity and writing type**, and **students’ and teachers’ attitudes**. These barriers combine to reduce the accuracy and usefulness of student feedback and weaken uptake. At the same time, students’ evaluative skills can be enhanced through **specific criteria and rubric-based instruction**, **practice routines that build confidence and accuracy**, and **explicit training to distinguish helpful from unhelpful feedback**. Assessment design and classroom support also matter: **structured formats and scaffolding**, **teacher modeling and guided practice**, and **grading and accountability** can make peer feedback more usable and engaging. Finally, student uptake is strongest when they have positive perceptions, relevant experiences, and strong feedback literacy [N1-F1][N2-R1][N4-F3][N6-R1][N6-R2][N6-R3][N3-F2][N3-R2].
